metadata.title: The Role of Teacher Autonomy, School Climate, and “Perceptions of Value & Policy Influence” in Predicting Lower Secondary School Teachers’ Job Satisfaction

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD TALIS 2018 core teacher data for South Africa, targeting lower secondary teachers (ISCED 2). The authors describe TALIS’s two-stage sampling (schools selected with probability proportional to size, then teachers randomly selected within schools), but they do not report whether TALIS sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in SPSS analyses. Because the analysis is based on Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple regression rather than PV-based achievement scaling, the paper does not document any PV-specific weighting workflow. Given the absence of explicit weight-variable reporting, the safest interpretation is that the authors either used unweighted analyses or relied on default SPSS handling without documenting TALIS complex-survey weight variables.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is teacher job satisfaction measured via Likert-scale items and aggregated subscales (JSENV, JSPRO), not a cognitive achievement score with TALIS plausible values. Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable for this outcome. The paper reports that all variables had missing data and provides N ranges, but it does not specify the missing-data handling method (e.g., listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, or imputation), which is a reporting gap for regression and correlation sample comparability.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 core teacher data for South Africa, restricted to lower secondary school teachers (ISCED 2). Participants were drawn using TALIS’s two-stage sampling design: systematic random sampling of schools with probability proportional to size, followed by random selection of teachers within sampled schools. The analysis reports variable-level missingness (e.g., teacher autonomy and disciplinary climate with the highest missing counts) and uses available N per variable in correlations and regression, but it does not explicitly state the missing-data rule.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 South Africa (Lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Model 1 R2=0.031 (ΔR2=0.031, β=0.177, p<.001). Model 2 R2=0.078 (ΔR2=0.047, p<.001). Model 3 R2=0.104 (ΔR2=0.026, p<.001). Correlations: autonomy r=0.179 (p<.01), disciplinary climate r=-0.185 (p<.01), teacher-student relations r=0.216 (p<.01), participation r=0.186 (p<.01), VALP r=0.184 (p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 South Africa (lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2) the study leveraged teacher autonomy, school climate subdimensions (participation among stakeholders, disciplinary climate, teacher-student relations), and perceptions of value & policy influence to predict job satisfaction with the profession, finding that teacher autonomy explained about 3% of the variance and the full hierarchical model explained about 10% (with VALP adding ~3%). This indicates that strengthening teachers’ autonomy and improving school climate—while also valuing teachers’ input in policy—may increase professional job satisfaction, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 South Africa (Lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2)
main_findings.target_variable: Job satisfaction with the work environment (JSENV)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Model 1 R2=0.045 (ΔR2=0.045, β=0.213, p<.001). Model 2 R2=0.311 (ΔR2=0.266, p<.001). Model 3 R2=0.315 (ΔR2=0.004, p<.001). Correlations: autonomy r=0.214 (p<.01), disciplinary climate r=-0.314 (p<.01), teacher-student relations r=0.413 (p<.01), participation r=0.490 (p<.01), VALP r=0.127 (p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 South Africa (lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2) the study leveraged teacher autonomy, participation among stakeholders, disciplinary climate, teacher-student relations, and perceptions of value & policy influence to predict job satisfaction with the work environment, finding that autonomy explained about 4.5% of the variance and school climate variables substantially increased explained variance to about 31% (with VALP adding only ~0.4%). This indicates that interventions targeting day-to-day school climate—especially stakeholder participation and teacher-student relations—are likely to be more impactful for work-environment satisfaction than societal/policy perceptions alone, while causality cannot be inferred.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 South Africa (Lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical multiple regression: Model 1 R2=0.054 (ΔR2=0.054, β=0.233, p<.001). Model 2 R2=0.261 (ΔR2=0.207, p<.001). Model 3 R2=0.277 (ΔR2=0.016, p<.001). Correlations (overall satisfaction): autonomy r=0.177 (p<.01), disciplinary climate r=-0.304 (p<.01), teacher-student relations r=0.385 (p<.01), participation r=0.423 (p<.01), VALP r=0.177 (p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 South Africa (lower secondary teachers, ISCED 2) the study leveraged teacher autonomy, participation among stakeholders, disciplinary climate, teacher-student relations, and perceptions of value & policy influence to predict overall job satisfaction, finding that autonomy explained about 5% of the variance and adding school climate increased explained variance to about 26% (with VALP adding ~2%). This indicates that policy and school leadership should jointly promote teacher autonomy and a supportive school climate, while also ensuring teachers feel valued and influential in policy processes to improve overall job satisfaction.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD TALIS 2018 core teacher data for South Africa, focusing on lower secondary teachers (ISCED 2; N=2046). Using Pearson correlations and hierarchical multiple regression in SPSS, it examines how teacher autonomy, school climate subdimensions (disciplinary climate, teacher-student relations, participation among stakeholders), and teachers’ perceptions of value & policy influence relate to job satisfaction (JSENV, JSPRO, and overall). The results show significant associations for all predictors except disciplinary climate in the abstract’s summary, with autonomy explaining roughly 3–5% of variance and school climate explaining substantially more (about 5–28% depending on the satisfaction dimension). Model fit is reported via R² and incremental ΔR² (e.g., overall satisfaction R²≈0.277 in Model 3). Limitations include cross-sectional self-report measurement, unspecified missing-data handling, and no documentation of TALIS complex-survey weighting, so findings should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
